entities.name: Charles II of Albret
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Charles II d'Albret (1407–1471), Viscount of Tartas and Lord of Albret, was a pivotal Gascon magnate whose military and administrative service solidified royal French authority in southwestern France during the tumultuous final decades of the Hundred Years' War. Succeeding his father, Charles I, who famously fell at Agincourt, Charles II inherited a vast seigneurial domain and a deep-seated allegiance to the Valois monarchy, positioning him as a crucial bulwark against English influence in the strategically vital region of Aquitaine. His career exemplifies the complex feudal loyalties and geopolitical struggles that defined late medieval Western Europe, ultimately contributing to the nascent formation of a unified French state.

As a seasoned commander, Charles II actively participated in the reconquest of Gascony, a series of campaigns fundamental to expelling English forces from their last continental strongholds. He played a significant role in the decisive Battle of Castillon in 1453, a French victory often cited as the effective end of the Hundred Years' War, where his forces contributed to the rout of John Talbot's English army. Beyond military exploits, d'Albret served as Lieutenant General of Guyenne, demonstrating his administrative acumen in governing newly re-secured territories and integrating them into the royal domain, navigating the intricate balance between local feudal rights and centralizing royal power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Charles II of Albret played a critical role in the final expulsion of English forces from France and the consolidation of royal authority in Gascony. His actions contributed directly to the end of the Hundred Years' War and the strengthening of the French monarchy, shaping the territorial integrity of modern France.
